title: Bond-operator analytical approach for the $t$-$J$ model
abstract: We present a bond-operator theory (BOT) for analytical consideration of the $t$-$J$ model and its extensions with longer-rage hopping terms. This technique is based on previously suggested representation of electron operators via localized spins 1/2 and spinless Fermi-operators of mobile holons which requires no constraint between them. We introduce a representation of operators of spins, holons, and electrons in (extended) unit cell containing several lattice sites via a zoo of Bose- and Fermi-operators acting in the Hilbert space of all quantum states of the whole unit cell. BOT provides a regular expansion of physical quantities in powers of $1/n$ using conventional diagrammatic technique, where $n\ge1$ is the maximum number of introduced quasiparticles (bosons and fermions) which can occupy a unit cell. The suggested representation reproduces commutation algebra of all operators at any $n>0$ and allows to consider both magnetically ordered and disordered phases. Some elementary excitations described in the BOT by separate bosons or fermions appear in common approaches as bound states of conventional quasiparticles. In particular, there are two-hole bound states (Cooper pairs of two holes) which are described within the BOT by separate bosons. We discuss in detail properties of the $t$-$J$ model on the square lattice with no more than two holes (polarons). Although the expansion parameter $1/n$ is not small in the physically meaningful case of $n=1$, we obtain a good quantitative agreement with previous numerical findings at $n=1$ even in the first order in $1/n$ after taking into account a few simple diagrams. Self-consistent calculations in the first order in $1/n$ bring our results to a very good quantitative agreement with previous numerical findings of the ground state energy, staggered magnetization, and spectra of magnons, polarons, and lowest-energy two-hole bound states.
summary: This paper introduces the Bond-Operator Theory (BOT) as an analytical framework to study the strongly correlated $t$-$J$ model. By reformulating electron operators using localized spins and holon fermions, BOT systematically expands physical quantities in powers of $1/n$. The theory successfully reproduces key magnetic and superconducting properties, showing strong quantitative agreement with state-of-the-art numerical simulations.
main_problem: The paper aims to develop an analytical, constraint-free theory for the $t$-$J$ model, which is crucial for understanding high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates.
main_result: The Bond-Operator Theory (BOT) provides a systematic expansion in powers of $1/n$, yielding quantitative agreement with advanced numerical methods for ground state energy and excitation spectra.
method: The core method is the Bond-Operator Theory, which reformulates electron operators using localized spins and mobile holon Fermi-operators to eliminate physical constraints inherent in simpler models.
model_or_system: The system studied is the one-band $t$-$J$ model on a square lattice, described by an effective Hamiltonian involving hopping ($t$) and exchange coupling ($J$). The theory handles both magnetically ordered and disordered phases.
key_observables: Ground state energy, staggered magnetization, magnon spectra, polaron spectrum, and two-hole bound state binding energies.
important_parameters: The expansion parameter is $1/n$, where $n$ relates to the maximum number of quasiparticles per unit cell. The model parameters are $t$ and $J$.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that physical quantities can be expanded as a regular series in powers of $1/n$; however, the first-order expansion is noted to be insufficient for full quantitative accuracy.
figures_summary: Figures compare calculated spectra (magnons, polarons) and spectral weights using BOT against results from Self-Consistent Born Approximation (SCBA), Exact Diagonalization (ED), and Green's Function Monte Carlo (GFMC).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the BOT formalism by mapping electron operators to spin/holon operators, derives the effective Hamiltonian, calculates observables via diagrammatic expansion in $1/n$, and compares results for various excitations (magnons, polarons) against established numerical benchmarks.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism/superconductivity, the use of an advanced operator formalism that systematically handles constraints and provides a controlled series expansion is valuable for theoretical physics dealing with complex many-body Hamiltonians.
